title: HP hot-plug RAID memory revived as a parity tier in 3D stacks
idea: HP's hot-plug RAID memory was dropped because it gave up 20-25% of capacity to redundancy. Inside a 3D DRAM or HBM stack, add one XOR parity tier per 16 data tiers plus a spare. When a tier fails, its data is rebuilt onto the spare in the background and the stack stays in service.
why: About 6% overhead to survive a whole-tier failure, raising 3D stack yield and life (facts 2, 6) with repair built in.

title: Spatial-ALD roll-to-roll steel foil deposits 64-tier stacks
idea: IFR: 'tiers deposit at newspaper speed.' Backward: run stainless-steel foil past spatial-ALD heads (precursor zones split by gas curtains, no pump-down cycles) to lay a 64-tier channel/dielectric superlattice continuously at meters per minute, then pattern vertical holes by roll nanoimprint and fill.
why: Capital (fact 4) and 3D deposition cost: ~10x lower deposition tool cost per tier than batch vacuum ALD/CVD on a cheap U.S.-available foil.

title: Known-good-tier lamination: binned two-tier oxide modules
idea: Under 400 C, fabricate two-tier oxide DRAM modules on cheap glass carriers, test and bin each one, then laminate only good modules by 250 C Cu-Cu hybrid bonding into 16-tier stacks. Modules are made in parallel, not in series.
why: Fact 2 and capital intensity: decouples stack yield from tier count and cuts cycle time about 8x versus sequential tier processing.

title: LTPO memory panel: polysilicon sense amps, oxide cells, one glass sheet
idea: IFR: 'periphery and array each get their perfect transistor.' Backward: copy the LTPO OLED backplane flow: laser-crystallized polysilicon (~100 cm2/Vs) on glass for sense amps, decoders and I/O, with low-leakage IGZO 2T gain cells stacked above, so one glass die holds fast periphery and long-retention cells.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and capital: periphery-under-array on the same sheet in existing display LTPO lines; seconds of retention cut refresh ~100x.

title: Transistorless crosspoint DRAM: threshold switch in series with capacitor
idea: Po: the array has no transistors. Each 4F2 crosspoint holds a MIM capacitor in series with an ovonic threshold switch that snaps on above ~1.5 V and is near-insulating below; half-select biasing writes and reads one cell, and the selector-capacitor pillar stacks in 4-8 decks like 3D XPoint but stores charge instead of phase.
why: Facts 2/4: 4F2 crosspoint with no lateral transistor sidesteps the 3D-DRAM transistor blocker; ~2 masks per deck gives ~3-5x bits per litho step. Risks: selector off-leakage sets retention and selector endurance must exceed 1e15.

title: Biologist's mitochondrial cristae: internally folded lateral capacitor
idea: Mitochondria fold their membranes to multiply area. Make each 3D DRAM tier a stack of 4 SiGe sub-layers with alternating Ge content, then use a Ge-selective lateral recess to corrugate the capacitor cavity walls before depositing the electrode and dielectric.
why: ~3x capacitor area for the same lateral length, so the horizontal capacitor shrinks and tier pitch tightens (Facts 1, 2).

title: Slipform tier growth: channels rise through self-aligned tiers
idea: Like slipform concrete poured as the forms climb, grow the vertical channel and the tier stack together: area-selective deposition lays each tier's dielectric and wordline everywhere except on the oxide-semiconductor channel stubs (an inhibitor monolayer binds only there), then selective ALD extends the channels by one tier; no deep hole etch and no per-tier lithography.
why: Eliminates the 60-100:1 vertical etch that caps 3D tier count (fact 2) and removes per-tier masks (fact 4); every tier is self-aligned, so tier count is limited by deposition time rather than etch.

title: Photomultiplier read: avalanche gain junction under each pillar
idea: Like a photomultiplier or SPAD turning one photon into a pulse, place a quenched avalanche junction at the foot of each vertical bitline biased just below breakdown; a 0.1 fF cell's few hundred electrons trigger ~100x multiplication, then a passive quench resets it, so cells and lines stay tiny.
why: Capacitor wall and access energy (facts 1, 8): Cs drops ~50x and the local line stays a few fF; claims >10x lower energy per read if avalanche statistics and dark counts are tamed.

title: Second array on the wafer backside sharing one periphery
idea: Worse: use only one face of the wafer and grind 700 um of silicon to dust. Flip: after building the front array and bonding to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, build a second low-thermal-budget array on the exposed backside, and tie both arrays to the same sense amps through nano-TSVs so every periphery block serves two arrays.
why: ~2x bits per wafer start and half the periphery area per bit (fact 7: periphery ~49% of die); halves quartz-crucible wafer demand per bit.

title: Per-tier pulsed plates replace the static half-VDD common plate
idea: Substitute the global static plate at VARY/2 with tier-segmented plates driven by periphery: during restore the plate is pulsed -0.5 V so a 0.6 V bitline swing stores today's 1.1 V-equivalent charge, and during read it is bumped to boost signal into the SA; in 3D each tier's plate is naturally a separate film.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): VARY ~1.0 -> 0.6 V cuts array CV² energy ~2.5x and lowers wordline boost (~3 -> 2.4 V).

title: Phosphorus monolayer doping uniformly dopes vertical pillar sidewalls without implant
idea: Graft a self-limiting monolayer of a phosphorus-bearing molecule (e.g., diethyl vinylphosphonate) onto HF-cleaned vertical Si pillars, cap with evaporated SiO2 and spike-anneal to drive a conformal ~1e20 cm^-3, few-nm-deep n+ layer into every sidewall and pillar top.
why: Forms source/drain and buried-bitline junctions on 4F2 pillars with atomic depth control, avoiding implant shadowing at high aspect ratio (fact 4) and narrowing junction-leakage spread (fact 3); needs a wet bench and RTA.

title: RDRAM lesson: move the whole periphery to a bonded logic wafer
idea: Rambus RDRAM died largely because fast I/O built in slow, leaky DRAM transistors cost die area, heat and price. Split the die: the array wafer carries only cells, bitlines and wordlines, and a separate logic-node wafer with the sense amps, decoders and PHY is hybrid-bonded underneath at about 1 um pitch. Each wafer is made in its best process.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7), so array efficiency rises to ~85%, and fast low-voltage logic cuts I/O energy. About 1.6x bits per array wafer.

title: Copper bond per bitline gives every bitline its own sense amp
idea: Hybrid-bond the cell-array wafer face-to-face to a logic wafer at ~0.4 um Cu pitch so every short local bitline (64 cells) lands on its own sense amplifier built in an advanced logic node, abolishing open/folded bitline sharing.
why: Moves the 49% periphery (fact 7) to dense logic, cuts Cb ~4x so Cs can drop toward 1-2 fF (fact 1), and per-bitline sensing enables column-granular activation that ends 128x overfetch (fact 8).

title: Anodized-cookware pores: AAO capacitor forests on 28 nm logic
idea: Anodize a thick aluminium BEOL layer on 28-40 nm logic wafers to self-organize 60-80 nm-pitch pores with AR >100:1, ALD TiN/high-k/TiN into them, and tie each pore cluster to a logic-node access transistor to make stand-alone 1T1C DRAM in foundries that never made DRAM.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AAO reaches AR 100+ by electrochemistry, not etch, for Cs >10 fF per cell, and it enlists U.S. trailing logic fabs with only a plating-bath module added.

title: Hybrid-bond pads double as sense-amp coupling capacitors
idea: In a wafer-on-wafer DRAM (array wafer face-bonded to a CMOS wafer), leave a 2-3 nm oxide in the Cu-Cu bond pads that carry 16:1-muxed local bitlines, so each pad is both the interconnect and the coupling capacitor of a charge-transfer preamp on the logic wafer. The bond needs no DC continuity, and the logic-side sense amp runs at 0.5 V.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7) and voltage floor (fact 10): sense amps leave the array wafer; low-voltage sensing claimed ~2x lower sensing energy and ~25% smaller array die.

title: Flood-gun self-restoring cells: global diode pump refreshes every bit
idea: Revive the Tektronix bistable storage tube, whose flood gun held every spot at one of two stable potentials without reading it: each cell gets a tiny vertical diode plus coupling-capacitor pump driven by a global AC 'flood' line, so leaked '1' cells are recharged and '0' cells clamped low, all in parallel without activating rows or sense amps.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth loss) with an array-wide, sense-free restore; refresh energy down ~5-10x.

title: Core-rope via-programmed 3D weight store, one sense per rope
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope, where a bit was set by whether a wire threaded a core: inference weights are encoded by whether a BEOL via links a rope wire to a shared sense node, written by maskless laser/e-beam via patterning in a mature U.S. fab and stacked 16 metal decks high, with one sense amp per 64 rope wires. Static weights leave DRAM, which keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are often >50% of inference DRAM; rope bits cost ~5-10x less than DRAM bits and need no EUV, capacitor or refresh.

title: Chain DRAM: series-connected cells eliminate per-cell bitline contacts
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying (from chain FeRAM and NAND strings): place each access transistor in parallel with its capacitor and chain 8-16 cells in series between a block-select device and the bitline. To read cell k, turn off only its transistor; its capacitor voltage then appears in series on the bitline through the conducting neighbors.
why: Fact 4: planar 4F2-class layout without vertical transistors or buried bitlines and ~8x fewer bitline contacts; ~30% smaller cell at the same F.

title: Monolayer MoS2 gain-cell tiers stacked by wafer-scale film transfer
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells and thin films: grow wafer-scale monolayer MoS2 on reusable sapphire templates and transfer the films one by one onto the stack below 300 C, each film becoming a tier of 2T0C cells. The 1.8 eV bandgap and 0.7 nm body give off-currents below ~1e-19 A/um, and with no capacitor the tier pitch can shrink to ~30 nm.
why: Fact 2 and 3: ~3x more tiers per um of stack height than capacitor-based 3D DRAM, retention of hours, no crucible-grown Si per tier.

title: Overlay-free crossbar cells from bonding two orthogonal line wafers
idea: [Box: MIM charge | two-terminal threshold selector (OTS/NbO2) | pulsed charge-share sensing | face-to-face bond of two line-grating wafers | Si | ArF SAQP gratings on each wafer] Wafer A carries bitline gratings capped with capacitor films, wafer B carries orthogonal wordline gratings capped with selector film; bonding them makes every crossing a 1S1C cell, and any overlay error only shifts the whole grid.
why: No EUV (fact 4): lines are the easiest ArF pattern and cells need no alignment, giving 4F2 at F~20 nm; selector leakage limits retention.

title: Plumber's pipes under the floor: backside bitlines for 4F2
idea: The plumber runs pipes in the basement, not across the living room. Build 4F2 vertical-channel transistors with the capacitor on top, then flip and thin the wafer and form the bitline from the backside, contacting the pillar bottoms directly.
why: Removes the buried metal bitline in a deep silicon trench, the hardest step of 4F2 VCT; bitline capacitance falls ~30% and pitch relaxes (Facts 1, 4).

title: Coaxial-cable cell: shell transistor wrapped around a core capacitor
idea: Scale a coaxial cable down to 40 nm: in one vertical hole, ALD an outer gate, gate oxide and oxide-semiconductor shell channel, then fill the core with a MIM capacitor, so the access transistor surrounds its own storage node. The bitline contacts the top of the shell and the bottom of the core is the plate, giving a 4F2 cell from one etch.
why: Takes 6F2 to 4F2 (fact 4) with one hole per cell instead of separate transistor and capacitor levels: ~33% less area per bit and fewer critical masks.

title: Optane's selector, not its PCM: OTS-gated capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's real breakthrough was the ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selector; what killed it as a DRAM substitute was slow, wearing phase-change material (PCM). Pair the OTS with a MIM capacitor (one selector, one capacitor) in stacked crosspoint decks. The OTS snaps on above threshold to charge or discharge the cap in nanoseconds and blocks under half-select, giving transistor-free DRAM cells of 4F2 per deck.
why: Removes the access transistor and EUV-patterned cell (facts 2, 4). Four to eight decks with shared litho could give ~4x density. Endurance is unlimited because no material changes state; shorter retention is the main risk.

title: Air-gap NEMS contact switch as zero-leakage 3D access device
idea: Electrostatic pull-in: in each tier, a laterally actuated Ru/TiN nanobeam, released from a sacrificial layer, replaces the lateral access transistor. In the off state a vacuum gap sits in series with the capacitor, so there is no subthreshold leakage tail at all.
why: Removes the ≤13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3); claim retention set only by dielectric leakage (minutes), so refresh energy falls ~90%. Contact endurance near 1e15 cycles is the big risk.

title: Liquid-nitrogen-only 3D DRAM with tenfold smaller lateral capacitors
idea: Design a 3D DRAM exclusively for 77 K immersion pods (LN2 is cheap, abundant and US-made): subthreshold leakage falls >10^6x, so a lateral cell with a ~0.5 fF capacitor that fits inside a 25 nm tier, paired with very short local bitlines, retains data for seconds.
why: Dissolves the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the 3D capacitor blocker (fact 2); refresh approaches zero (fact 3) and tier pitch roughly halves, ~2x tiers per stack height, with cooling cost offset by lower wire resistance and no refresh.

title: Aluminum anodization pores template litho-free vertical 4F2 cells
idea: Anodize a 300 nm sputtered Al film on Si in oxalic acid (two-step, seeded by a sparse e-beam pre-pattern for long-range order) to form a hexagonal pore array at 40-60 nm pitch, then ALD a ZTO shell channel, Al2O3 dielectric and TiN core gate down each pore with the capacitor on top.
why: Defines a 4F2 vertical array by electrochemistry and ALD alone, with no EUV (fact 4) and minimal masks; a beaker, power supply and ALD tool suffice.

title: Dual-ended mirror pillar stores two bits per 4F2 footprint
idea: IFR: 'two cells in the space of one.' Backward: build a vertical channel pillar with one capacitor on top (front side) and another at its bottom (after backside thinning), split the gate into independent upper and lower half-gates, and tap the shared bitline at the pillar midpoint.
why: Density (fact 4): ~2F2 effective cell without shrinking F, ~1.8x bits per wafer at the same litho.

title: Plated-pillar memory: circumferential magnetization lining 3D NAND-style holes
idea: Revive Univac/Bell plated-wire memory vertically: etch high-AR holes through a stack of word-strap tiers, ALD a soft magnetic shell, spacer and reference layer down each hole, and store bits as circumferentially magnetized ring segments under each strap, sensed non-destructively by the magnetoresistance of an axial read current. Closed-flux rings have no stray field, so hole pitch can be tight.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a deposition-built 3D cell with non-destructive read, no capacitor and near-unlimited endurance; 3D NAND-like density at ~20-50 ns reads.

title: Turbine-blade eutectic solidification grows built-in vertical nanorod plates
idea: Borrowed from directionally solidified eutectic alloys used in turbine blades: solidify a Si-TaSi2 eutectic ingot so billions of aligned metallic TaSi2 nanorods run through monocrystalline Si, then slice wafers in which each rod is a ready-made vertical capacitor plate or buried bitline, with cells formed around them by one mask.
why: Self-organized vertical conductors replace high-AR etch and fill (facts 1,4); a ~100x path if fast growth brings rod pitch near ~100 nm; trade-off: irregular lattice needs per-die mapping.

title: Drum-era SOAP placement makes shift-register memories act random-access
idea: Revive the IBM 650's Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each next instruction where the rotating drum would be when needed: a compiler/controller lays out tensors, KV-cache pages and weights in shift-register arrays (CCD strings, racetracks, delay loops) so the next word reaches the read port just in time, with out-of-order prefetch hiding the rest.
why: Lets transistor-free serial 3D arrays serve the predictable ~60-80% of AI memory traffic at effective 10-30 ns latency, unlocking 5-10x denser arrays for DRAM's job.

title: Wafer-on-edge stack: deposition thickness sets the cell pitch
idea: Inverts 'the array is patterned face-up by lithography.' Deposit ~300 alternating Si/SiO2 (or n+/p) layer pairs, saw the wafer into slabs, rotate each slab 90 degrees and bond its cut edge to a logic wafer, so film thickness rather than EUV sets one cell pitch; only the orthogonal pitch is patterned, by coarse litho on the exposed edge.
why: Litho/capital wall (fact 4): removes EUV from one of the two pitch axes (~10 nm pitch from deposition control); could cut 5-7 EUV layers to ~2-3 and cost/bit ~20-30%.

title: Accordion: origami-fold one thinned wafer into an 8-tier stack
idea: Random stimulus 'accordion' forced onto stacking: build a planar DRAM array on a wafer thinned to ~5 um on a polyimide carrier, leaving 200 um flexible RDL 'hinge' strips between array panels, then fold the strip like bellows so 8 panels stack face-to-back. Bitline and I/O buses run continuously through the hinges, so the stack needs no TSVs and no per-layer bonding.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and per-layer bond yield: no TSV keep-out and no die-to-die alignment; claim wafer area per stacked bit -30 to -50% versus HBM, and lower capital per stacked GB.

title: 2050 engineer slices deposited superlattice edge-on as array
idea: Deposit a 400-layer stack of alternating 8 nm channel and isolation films, dice it into bars, rotate them 90 degrees and hybrid-bond the polished cut face onto CMOS. Every film edge becomes a channel row, so film thickness sets one axis of the array pitch; the perpendicular wordlines are patterned with DUV pitch-split.
why: Takes EUV off one array axis because the pitch comes from deposition (sub-10 nm is possible); ~2-3x density at DUV cost (Fact 4).

title: Inductor ping-pong moves charge from closing to opening wordline
idea: Connect the wordline being closed to the next wordline being opened through a shared on-die or interposer inductor for one LC half-cycle, so the 3 V charge transfers almost entirely instead of being dumped to ground, then top off the remainder from the pump.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): direct charge sharing between equal capacitors recovers at most 50%, but a resonant half-cycle recovers ~80% of CV^2; with a ~3 V wordline swing, pumped wordline energy and charge-pump losses fall several-fold.

title: Slime-mould via mesh: training pulses burn out shorted bond paths
idea: Bond memory dies through an over-provisioned mesh of 2-4 redundant micro-vias per signal, each with a thin series fuse link (like Physarum's initial diffuse network); a post-bond training current sequence blows the fuse on any via drawing excess current through a bridging short, leaving the reinforced healthy paths as the final network.
why: HBM TSV/bond yield tax (20-30% loss): turns bridging and single-via defects into self-repaired links; could recover ~10-15 points of stack yield without spare dies.

title: Capillary self-alignment for mass-parallel die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: dispense a sub-uL water film on hydrophilic bond sites ringed by hydrophobic borders, drop DRAM dies with a fast coarse pick-and-place, and let surface tension pull each die to <200 nm alignment. Hybrid bonds form as the film evaporates, placing thousands of dies per minute.
why: Fact 6: cuts HBM stacking cost and time, enables finer bond pitch (cheaper TSVs) and known-good-die everywhere; could lift HBM stack yield 10-20 points.

title: Lotus-leaf droplets: capillary self-assembly bonds memory tiles onto logic
idea: Water beads align on a lotus leaf: put a droplet on each hydrophilic bond site of a logic wafer, release thousands of small (1-2 mm2) known-good DRAM tiles in fluid, and let surface tension pull each tile to <0.5 um alignment before it direct-bonds as the water evaporates. No fine-alignment die-to-wafer bonder is needed.
why: 3D integration capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): batch fluidic placement at >10k tiles/hour replaces $10M+ D2W bonders, making memory-on-logic cheap.

title: Disulfide-staple pillars stitch all tiers against 125 C creep
idea: Thermophile proteins add disulfide bonds and salt bridges to stay folded when hot; add dense SiCN 'staple' plugs etched through all tiers every few microns in dummy regions and anchored into the substrate, mechanically clamping the stack so CTE mismatch at 125 C cannot drive delamination or slow creep of contacts over 10 years.
why: 3D stack integrity at high temperature: suppresses delamination and creep-driven contact drift so 100+ tier stacks can meet grade-1 life for <1% area.

title: Silicon seed-window lateral overgrowth grows each crystalline tier in place
idea: Over each finished tier, deposit oxide, open a sparse grid of seed windows to the crystalline tier below and grow Si by selective epitaxial lateral overgrowth until fronts merge, then CMP to 30 nm; merge seams are laid out under wordline-cut and dummy regions.
why: Single-crystal stacked tiers without bonding or germanium (fact 2); periphery is hybrid-bonded later so the epi thermal budget is tolerable, and the array layout is co-designed around seam locations.

title: Mangrove salt glands: hydrogen-getter wells drain each oxide tier
idea: Mangroves excrete salt through dedicated leaf glands; place Ti/Pd-capped getter 'glands' (small trenches of hydrogen-absorbing metal) every few microns in each tier of an oxide-semiconductor 3D array so hydrogen diffusing at 125 C flows into sinks instead of donor-doping the channels.
why: Hydrogen-driven Vt shift is the main 10-yr high-temperature failure of oxide channels; getter wells could hold drift <50 mV over 10 yrs at 125 C, making low-leakage oxide 3D tiers automotive-grade.

title: Weimer's 1962 TFT reborn: panel-fab memory on Gen-8 glass
idea: Revive RCA's thin-film transistor for memory: build 4-tier oxide-TFT DRAM-like arrays on Gen-8.5 glass in idle LCD and plasma panel fabs at ~1 um features, accept 1% defective cells across huge panels with block codes, and sell them as cheap capacity modules.
why: Capital intensity and U.S./allied manufacturability: panel fabs cost ~100x less per m2 than DRAM wafers; at 4 tiers cost could approach ~$10/GB with no EUV or quartz crucibles.

title: Sixteen-cell micro-bitlines with per-tier oxide-TFT sense latches
idea: Po: every cell has a sense amp next door. In each oxide-semiconductor tier place a 4-TFT latch every 16 cells along the bitline so local bitline capacitance falls from ~60 fF to ~2 fF; latches drive a global bitline down to the base die.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): with Cb/Cs held at 2-4, Cs can be 0.5-1 fF and planar inside the tier, removing the tall capacitor that blocks 3D.

title: KV-cache on display glass: mist-CVD oxide memory tiles from LCD fabs
idea: KV-cache buyers care about cost per bit far more than bits per mm2; build 3-tier oxide-channel 2T gain-cell arrays at relaxed 80 nm features on 2.2 x 2.5 m display glass in idle LCD fabs, depositing channels by atmospheric mist-CVD or nitrogen-purged ALD instead of argon-sputtered IGZO. Slice the panels into memory tiles hybrid-bonded to a logic bridge.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): display-fab area costs ~100x less per cm2 than DRAM wafer area, so even ~30x lower density gives several-fold cheaper bits for KV tiers, with no argon.

title: Silicon-oxygen HSQ resist becomes the patterned inter-tier dielectric directly
idea: Spin hydrogen silsesquioxane, write cell-isolation and inter-tier oxide patterns by e-beam, develop, and cure it into a SiO2-like dielectric that stays in the device, so each tier's isolation is written rather than deposited, masked and etched; repeat per tier on alignment marks.
why: Drops deposition, hardmask and etch steps per tier (fact 4), avoids plasma damage to channels (fact 3), and lets a university e-beam tool prototype multi-tier arrays at ~10 nm features.

title: Co-fired tiers: deposit all oxide channels amorphous, activate once
idea: Like co-firing green ceramic tapes in one kiln pass, deposit every tier's oxide-semiconductor channel and high-k amorphous at room temperature, then run one final anneal for the whole stack instead of annealing each tier and re-baking the lower tiers N times.
why: Accumulated thermal budget drifts lower-tier threshold voltage and leakage (facts 2, 3); one co-fire makes tier N match tier 1 and removes N-1 anneals (~20-30% cycle time).

title: Dual threshold ladders select one tier, deleting the 3D staircase
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: give each tier's lateral access device two series gates whose thresholds are graded in opposite directions through the stack (front-gate Vt rising with tier number, back-gate Vt falling). Driving the shared vertical front and back gates to the level pair for tier k turns on only tier k (tiers <=k AND >=k), so 8-16 tiers share one contact instead of a staircase.
why: Fact 2 and 7: staircase/contact area grows linearly with tier count; a 16-level ladder cuts staircase area and tier-contact masks ~10x, helping cross the 26-tier break-even.

title: Magnetostrictive-piezo laminate receivers replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Magnetostriction: each thinned die carries micro-coils that transmit, and FeGa/AlN magnetoelectric laminate pads that receive. The stray AC field from the die below strains the magnetostrictive layer, and the piezo layer turns that strain into a mV-scale voltage. The laminate's high field-to-voltage gain allows smaller-pitch, higher-bandwidth contactless links than plain inductive coils.
why: Removes TSVs and their keep-out zones (HBM TSV tax ~3x area and 20-30% yield loss, fact 6); claim recovers 15-25% die area and stacks known-good dies with no through-silicon etch.

title: Catt-spiral wafer-scale stacks bonded without known-good-die sorting
idea: Revive Trilogy/Anamartic wafer-scale integration and Ivor Catt's self-configuring spiral: wafer-to-wafer bond 8 whole DRAM wafers; at power-up tiles self-test and chain into a spiral that bypasses dead tiles, while live tiles tolerate up to 1% failing cells through local codes.
why: Facts 4 and 6: no dicing, known-good-die test or per-die TSV assembly; W2W stacking cost per bit drops ~20-30% and compound stack-yield loss disappears.

title: Diagonal sense-wire bitline twisting across tiers for 4F2 open arrays
idea: Copy core memory's diagonal sense wire, which crossed cores in alternating polarity so half-select pickup cancelled: in a vertical-channel 4F2 array, each bitline pair swaps tier position and coupling polarity every 8 cells, so wordline kick and neighbor coupling arrive as common-mode at the sense amp. This gives folded-bitline noise immunity at open-bitline area.
why: Facts 1 and 4: ~30-40% less coupling noise lets Cs drop from ~5 fF toward ~3.5 fF (lower capacitor aspect ratio) while keeping 4F2 (33% less area than 6F2).

title: Seesaw: vertical twin cell holds each bit across two tiers
idea: A seesaw rises on one side as it falls on the other: in a 3D die each bit is complementary charge on two cells stacked directly above one another on a vertical bitline pair, sensed differentially. The signal doubles and leakage is common-mode, so cheap tiers buy far longer retention behind a standard DDR5/LPDDR5 interface.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capacitor wall (fact 1): 2x signal allows ~0.5x Cs per cell (shorter capacitors) and 4-8x longer retention; the 2x cell cost is paid in tiers.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching carves single-crystal VCT pillar forests
idea: [Box: MIM charge | single-crystal Si VCT | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | DSA-patterned Pt/Au catalyst mesh + HF/H2O2 MacEtch] A perforated noble-metal mesh sinks into Si in HF/H2O2 and leaves straight, plasma-damage-free 20 nm pillars at AR >50, which become the vertical channels.
why: No EUV (fact 4) and leakage tail (fact 3): damage-free sidewalls trim the trap-assisted leakage tail, and wet tools cost far less than plasma etch.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 200:1 capacitor holes in a beaker
idea: Let a nanoscale metal catalyst do a plasma tool's job: pattern a perforated gold mesh with 180-nm litho plus spacer shrink, then immerse it in HF/H2O2. The metal sinks into the silicon and carves vertical holes at aspect ratios >200:1 for deep capacitors or vertical bitlines, with no plasma tool.
why: The capacitor charge wall wants AR ~115 (fact 1); MACE reaches it on a wet bench and slashes etch capital.

title: Silver-catalyzed chemical etch drills 200:1 vertical silicon pillars
idea: Pattern a perforated Ag film by e-beam lift-off, immerse in HF/H2O2 so the Ag sinks into the Si, and carve smooth vertical pillars or holes at aspect ratios >200:1 with no plasma, used as vertical channels and deep capacitor electrodes.
why: Breaks the capacitor aspect-ratio wall (fact 1 needs AR ~115) with a beaker-cost wet etch and no plasma damage to worsen the leakage tail (fact 3); Ag use is nanograms per wafer.

title: LCD panel fabs make DRAM by the square meter on glass
idea: Adapted from TFT-LCD backplanes (an LCD pixel is literally a 1T1C DRAM cell): run 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on 3 m x 3 m Gen-10.5 glass in idle display fabs, reach ~375 nm features with self-aligned quadruple spacers, and stack 8 TFT tiers; accept 200-500 ns access and a heavy refresh budget.
why: ~1.2 Mb/mm2 per tier x 8 tiers x 9 m2 is ~10 TB per panel for ~$1-2k, about $0.1-0.2/GB, ~50-100x below 2026 DRAM; no EUV, no quartz crucibles.

title: Split the cell across wafers: capacitors bonded onto transistors
idea: Fabricate storage capacitors on a separate wafer where perovskite (Ba,Sr)TiO3 can be crystallized at 650-750 C (k~100-300), then bond it face-to-face onto the transistor wafer through a self-aligning nano-pad lattice and strip the capacitor carrier. Transistor and capacitor never share a thermal budget.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): k>100 means AR <20 for 5 fF, removing the AR-115 requirement; the real risk is ~50 nm-pitch bonding versus today's ~400 nm.

title: Croissant lamination: tier doubling by repeated wafer fold-and-bond
idea: Like laminated dough that doubles its layers with every fold, grow an 8-tier Si/SiGe superlattice once, then bond the wafer face-to-face onto a copy of itself, Smart-Cut the donor and repeat, so four bond cycles give 128 tiers. No single epitaxy run ever exceeds the SiGe strain-relaxation limit, and each tier keeps single-crystal quality for the lateral transistor.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM cell (fact 2): the 26+ tier break-even stalls on strain and defects in thick superlattices; exponential tier count with log2 bonding steps claims >100 tiers in ~4-5 bonds.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM: bond whole undiced array wafer onto logic wafer
idea: Inverts 'the die is the product unit.' Hybrid-bond an undiced 300 mm DRAM array wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer, route around bad reticles in the logic, and ship the bonded pair as a ~2 TB memory slab with no scribe lines, pads, packages or TSVs.
why: Facts 5-6: kills HBM's ~3x area TSV tax and the package, gives ~PB/s internal bandwidth at <1 pJ/bit, and recovers ~10% wafer area lost to scribe and pads.

title: Unsawn wafer-scale memory slab bonded to a logic wafer
idea: Worse: dice, package and TSV-stack small dies, losing kerf, pads and 20-30% stack yield. Flip: hybrid-bond an entire array wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer, keep it whole, and route around failed tiles with a programmable on-wafer mesh, so no dicing, packaging or HBM TSVs are needed.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, fact 6) and package cost, recovers ~10% area from kerf and pads, and gives <0.5 pJ/bit links versus 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Whole DRAM wafer bonded onto a wafer-scale accelerator
idea: Wafer-scale computers already route around defects; hybrid-bond an undiced 300 mm DRAM wafer face-to-face onto a wafer-scale accelerator with bonds at every compute tile and map out bad mats in the routing fabric. Each tile reads the DRAM directly above it over millimeter-scale wires.
why: Data movement (fact 5): 3-4 pJ/bit HBM to ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit; HBM TSV tax (fact 6), dicing and packaging removed; ~1 TB at multi-TB/s per wafer.

title: Anamartic wafer-scale memory revived with hybrid-bonded Catt spiral routing
idea: Anamartic's Wafer Stack (Ivor Catt's spiral that threads good dies past bad ones) died on the cost of 1980s wafer-level interconnect. Hybrid-bond an undiced DRAM wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer that carries the spiral self-test router. At power-up each subarray tests itself and the router chains every good one into one address space, giving a 300 mm memory slab with no dicing, packaging or TSVs.
why: Removes packaging, test and TSV cost (fact 6) and off-chip I/O energy, since all traffic stays on-wafer (fact 5). All good silicon is harvested. Claims about 30-40% lower cost per bit than HBM for AI racks.

title: Wafer-scale stitched DRAM plane bonded to wafer-scale compute
idea: Limit: no reticle boundary and no dicing. Stitch array tiles across a full 300 mm wafer with redundant tile routing, then hybrid-bond the whole memory wafer face-to-face onto a wafer-scale compute wafer.
why: Facts 5 and 6: tens of PB/s of vertical bandwidth at sub-0.5 pJ/bit with no package, interposer or TSV overhead.

title: Ion-track membranes: particle-drilled pores averaged into capacitor cells
idea: IFR: 'pores drilled by particles, with no lithography.' Backward: irradiate a polyimide or glass sheet with swift heavy ions (~1e10-1e11 tracks/cm2), etch the latent tracks into ~20 nm pores 1-2 um deep, ALD-coat electrode/high-k/electrode, and bond a periodic TFT pad grid on top so each pad collects ~10 random pores whose capacitance averages statistically.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): tens of fF per cell with no etch tool, enough for 2-3 bits per cell; randomness is handled by averaging, not alignment.

title: Series-stacked array voltage domains recycle bitline charge between tiers
idea: Combine two arrays (bonded tiers) in series between 0 and 2xVARY: the upper array swings VARY-2VARY and its restore current returns through the lower array swinging 0-VARY, recycling charge like stacked-voltage logic, with the scheduler balancing activations.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~40-50% of array CV2 supply energy recycled without lowering VARY; fewer pumps shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: RV 12-volt rule: short pillars let the array run at 0.35 V
idea: Low-voltage DC works in RVs because the runs are short; build vertical-bitline mats with 32-cell bitlines (Cb ~1.5 fF), giving a charge-transfer ratio near 0.6 that supports sensing at VARY 0.35 V with a ~100 mV signal, with sense amps in a bonded low-voltage logic wafer.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): V from 1.0 to 0.35 V gives ~8x on CV2 and Cb is ~50x smaller than planar bitlines; claims >10x lower array energy per access.

title: Periphery outsourced to US mature-node wafers bonded under array
idea: IFR: 'the DRAM fab only makes array.' Backward: split each die into a pure-array wafer (cells and bitlines only) and a periphery wafer (charge pumps, wordline drivers, I/O) made at a U.S. 28-90 nm foundry, then hybrid-bond them, so the array fab drops all high-voltage and logic steps.
why: Periphery (fact 7), capital (fact 4), U.S. manufacturability: ~40% less leading-edge wafer area per bit, with half the value-add moved into existing U.S. mature fabs.

title: Capacitor that switches itself: Mott-selector-in-capacitor crosspoint
idea: Fold the transistor's role into the capacitor stack: metal / high-k / NbO2 Mott threshold layer / metal, where the Mott layer snaps conductive above ~1 V to charge the cell and returns insulating below, forming a transistor-free 1S1C crosspoint that can be stacked in BEOL.
why: 4F2 crosspoint stacking (facts 2,4); honest catch: selector off-current must fall below ~1e-17 A for ms retention, so first use is a us-retention refresh-heavy cache tier.

title: Hitachi PLEDM revived: h-BN barrier write transistor stacked on read gate
idea: Hitachi's 1990s PLEDM gain cell stacked a vertical multi-tunnel-barrier write transistor on the read transistor's gate, but died on leakage variability in its Si/SiN barriers. Rebuild the stacked write device with atomically uniform h-BN tunnel barriers so the storage node (the read gate) leaks below 1 aA. The result is a two-transistor gain cell in a one-transistor footprint.
why: No capacitor (fact 1), non-destructive read (fact 8), and retention long enough to cut refresh ~100x (fact 3), at ~4F2.

title: Fold one large planar array membrane into stacked layers
idea: [Box: 1T1C | planar IGZO | standard SA | accordion-folded thin-film membrane | polyimide on glass carrier | DUV-only planar process + laser lift-off + folding] Process one large array as a planar thin film with wiring continuous across fold lines, lift it off, and fold it accordion-style into 8-32 adhesive-bonded layers; interlayer connections are just the wires running around the folds.
why: Density per footprint without EUV: area becomes height, with no TSVs (fact 6) and no tier-by-tier alignment.

title: Tungsten-free plated copper staircases with self-forming barriers
idea: Under 400 C, fill all staircase contacts and vertical straps by room-temperature electroplated CuMn. A 300 C anneal self-forms a 2 nm MnSiOx barrier, so no W CVD is used anywhere in the 3D array.
why: Tungsten chokepoint: removes W from 3D wiring with about 3x lower contact resistance for tall stacks.

title: Car e-coat for capacitors: self-limiting electrophoretic high-k fill
idea: Automotive e-coating paints car bodies conformally because the deposited film insulates and halts further deposition; apply electrophoretic deposition of 3-5 nm SrTiO3/BaTiO3 nanocrystals into high-AR capacitor holes, field-driven and self-limiting, followed by a low-temperature densification anneal.
why: Reaches the k ~70 dielectric that fact 1 says is needed inside AR >100 structures where perovskite ALD struggles, faster and cheaper than ALD cycles; leakage along nanocrystal boundaries is the risk.

title: Z-critical cell puts every sub-20 nm dimension in film thickness
idea: Build stacked source/sacrificial/drain layers and later replace the sacrificial layer through a slit with channel, gate dielectric and wrap gate, so channel length, oxide, capacitor gap and wordline spacing are all set by ALD or epitaxy thickness and lithography prints only features of 40 nm or more.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): film thickness is controlled to ~0.1 nm for the cost of a deposition, so 5-7 EUV layers can fall to zero using ArF immersion, removing the single-supplier EUV chokepoint and much of the depreciation.

title: Optane's abandoned threshold-switch stack reused for capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: Revive the shelved 3D XPoint selector process: pair an Ovonic threshold switch with a tiny MIM capacitor (1S1C) in stacked crosspoint decks so the selector replaces the access transistor; OTS threshold scatter and leakage cause ~1% cell errors that tile-level codes correct.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: stackable charge cells with no transistors, built on existing deck-process know-how; 4 decks give ~4x bits per mask set.

title: Lay the capacitor flat and laminate it: MLCC-in-cell
idea: Replace the tall cylinder with a nanoscale multilayer ceramic capacitor: 6-10 alternating TiN/ZrO2 layers ALD-deposited laterally into a recess, with even electrodes tied to the storage node at one sidewall and odd ones to the plate at the other via selective alternating recess. Capacitance scales with layer count, not aspect ratio.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and lateral 3D tiers (fact 2): ~5 fF in a short footprint with no litho for added capacitance, only ALD cycles.

title: Smart-cut silicon carbide tier replaces silicon access transistors
idea: Substitute the silicon access-transistor layer with a ~200 nm 4H-SiC layer transferred from a reusable SiC donor (as SmartSiC does for power devices) and bonded over the capacitor array; 3.26 eV bandgap and ~1e-9 cm^-3 intrinsic carrier density (vs 1e10 in Si) suppress junction/GIDL leakage, while low mobility is irrelevant for an access device.
why: Leakage tail forces refresh (fact 3): retention 64 ms -> seconds-minutes, cutting refresh power (16-33% of idle) and the 10-20% bandwidth loss by ~95%.

title: Sourdough starter: one reusable donor wafer seeds every single-crystal tier
idea: Keep one starter and bake many loaves: grow porous-Si plus epi-Si on a premium Czochralski donor, split off a 50 nm single-crystal layer for each 3D DRAM tier, then re-polish and regrow the donor 10-20 times. Each stacked tier uses only a fraction of a newly pulled wafer.
why: Scarce resources: Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (>80%) and CZ wafer supply; claim ~10x fewer pulled wafers per tier, plus thin, high-quality channels for 3D (fact 2).

title: Layer-transferred 4H-SiC access transistors for hour-scale retention
idea: [Box: MIM charge | 4H-SiC MOSFET | charge-share SA | Smart Cut SiC film onto array wafer | reusable SiC donor | high-temperature activation before bonding] Transfer thin 4H-SiC films (3.26 eV gap, intrinsic carriers ~1e-9 cm^-3) from a reusable donor and build access transistors whose junction and GIDL leakage sit orders below Si, so cells refresh every minutes to hours.
why: Refresh (fact 3): recovers 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth, and permits smaller Cs (fact 1).

title: Shipbuilder's reusable donor hull: fifty Smart-Cut tiers per wafer
idea: Shipyards reuse the same slipway. Implant hydrogen into one thick bulk donor, bond it, cleave a 60 nm single-crystal Si tier, CMP the donor and repeat ~50 times. Each tier gets its transistors at <=450C.
why: Gives single-crystal channel tiers for 3D DRAM, and one Czochralski wafer feeds 50 tiers, cutting high-purity quartz crucible demand per bit ~50x.

title: Transistorless 1S1C crosspoint: threshold switch guards each capacitor
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM cell needs an access transistor.' Put a volatile ovonic threshold switch in series with a small MIM capacitor at every crosspoint of stackable 4F² line layers; full-select pulses exceed threshold to read/write, half-selected cells stay off, and decks stack like 3D XPoint.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 4F² per deck times N decks with no lateral transistor; OTS off-leakage (~pA) forcing ms-scale refresh is the honest risk.

title: Geological-strata scheduling: map data lifetime to each tier's measured retention
idea: Treat a 3D stack like sediment strata, each tier with its own retention from process variation: measure every tier's retention at test and expose it to the memory controller. The controller puts short-lived data (activations, KV-cache that dies within 50 ms) in leaky tiers that never need refresh and long-lived data in strong tiers.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and 3D yield: tiers that would fail retention binning become usable, and refresh drops ~2-5x.

title: Transistorless crosspoint DRAM with wide-bandgap Schottky selector and capacitor
idea: IFR: 'no access transistor, so cells stack like crosspoint.' Backward: replace the transistor with a two-terminal back-to-back Schottky selector in a wide-bandgap oxide (e.g., Ga2O3 with Pt contacts) targeting ~1e-19 A half-select leakage, in series with a small MIM capacitor, stacked as 1S1C crosspoint decks of only word and bit lines.
why: 4F2 and 3D without lateral transistors (facts 2, 4): ~2 masks per deck and ~4x density at the same F, if the selector's ~1e12 on/off ratio holds.

title: Thermophile S-layer protein crystals template sub-10 nm cell pitch
idea: Self-assemble an archaeal S-layer protein lattice (2D crystals with 10-13 nm unit cells) on the wafer inside coarse DUV guide frames, convert it to an inorganic AlOx hard mask by sequential infiltration synthesis, and etch vertical access pillars at that pitch: nature's own crystalline lithography.
why: Litho-bound scaling and EUV dependence: sub-EUV pitch with zero EUV exposures; 4F2 vertical cells at very small F could give several-x bits per area if defectivity is controlled.

title: Lighthouse: infrared beams through silicon replace TSV fields between dies
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm the way air is to a lighthouse beam: put micro-LED or VCSEL emitters and Ge photodiodes at matching metal-free windows on thinned stacked dies, so each link beams straight through several dies to its receiver. Hundreds of wide optical channels replace thousands of TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no metal vias through cell dies; claim 10-15% less die area per bit and +10 points stack yield, at ~1 pJ/bit link energy.

title: Eliminate cell-level lithography: vapour-deposited, plasma-developed block copolymer holes
idea: Deposit a block copolymer film from vapour (iCVD) that self-assembles into a hexagonal hole array at the 4F2 pitch, guided by the transistor topography, and develop it by dry plasma removal of one block, with no spin coat, aqueous develop or wet strip.
why: Water and EUV: replaces the capacitor-hole EUV layer and its develop/strip water with a dry self-assembly step; ~10x less water for that layer and one fewer EUV pass.

title: Stack-only U.S. fab: domestic 3D integration of imported array wafers
idea: Limit: no new DRAM front-end fab for three years. Fund U.S. hybrid-bonding and tier-stacking lines that buy array and periphery wafers from several allied sources and do all 3D integration, test and redundancy remap domestically.
why: U.S. manufacturability (about 1-2% share): captures the highest-value 3D step in 18-24 months at a fraction of front-end capital.

title: Through-silicon infrared beams with retro-modulators replace HBM TSVs
idea: Silicon's infrared transparency: the HBM base die holds InP micro-emitters whose 1.3 µm beams pass straight through thinned silicon dies to Ge photodiodes on each memory die (downlink). For the uplink, each memory die modulates the reflection of a base-die beam with an electro-absorption retro-modulator, so the DRAM dies need no lasers.
why: Removes the TSV tax and its yield loss (fact 6) and cuts movement energy (fact 5); claim <1 pJ/bit vertical links and ~3x less area per bit than TSV HBM.

title: Fractal H-tree bitlines equalize RC across every tier
idea: Bring the scale-invariant branching of lungs and trees into the array: route bitlines as a 3D H-tree so every cell in a 64-tier subarray is the same wire length from its sense amp. Bitline capacitance per sense amp then grows ~sqrt(N) instead of N.
why: Bitline-to-cell capacitance ratio versus small Cs (fact 1) and periphery share (fact 7): 2-4x more cells per sense amp at the same signal margin.

title: Hot-wall batch epitaxy grows a hundred superlattice wafers per run
idea: Worse: grow 200-period Si/SiGe stacks one wafer at a time for hours in single-wafer RPCVD. Flip: grow the superlattice in a hot-wall UHV-CVD/LPCVD batch furnace holding ~100 wafers, using fast gas-pulse switching for abrupt interfaces and in-situ X-ray reflectometry on a witness wafer.
why: Epitaxy cost per wafer for a 200-tier stack falls ~30-50x, keeping the 10x-density stack inside today's wafer cost envelope (facts 2, 4).

title: Periphery sandwich: mature-node CMOS bonded to arrays on both faces
idea: Worse: give every array a private periphery built in the expensive DRAM process. Flip: fabricate a 28 nm-class CMOS periphery wafer with hybrid-bond pads on both faces (via backside nTSVs), bond one cell-only array wafer above and one below, and time-share each sense amp between the upper and lower bitline through an isolation switch.
why: Periphery moves to cheap depreciated nodes and is amortized over two arrays: periphery area per bit -50% and the array wafer becomes cell-only (fact 7, fact 4 capital).

title: Light-through-glass optical buses replace vias between stacked dies
idea: IFR: 'tiers talk with no wire between them.' Backward: in a stack of thin transparent glass memory dies, put transfer-printed micro-LED emitters and oxide photodiodes in aligned columns with metal-free windows, so each die sends and receives its data bus optically straight through the dies above and below.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSVs or bonds in the data path and dies are swappable; ~0.5 pJ/bit at 1-10 Gb/s per channel, thousands of channels per die.

title: Periphery sandwiched between two array wafers, bitline pairs across bonds
idea: Reverse the CMOS-under-array order: thin the periphery wafer and hybrid-bond array wafers to BOTH faces (one face-down above, one face-up below). Each sense amplifier takes its true bitline from the upper array and its complement/reference bitline from the lower array, so one SA stripe and one decoder set serve two arrays.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): periphery silicon per bit halves (~1.6-1.8x bits per periphery-wafer area); arrays get unrestricted thermal budget; mirrored open-bitline pairs see matched noise.

title: Thousand-tier monolithic stack of atom-thin transistor sheets
idea: Po: tiers are counted in thousands, not tens. Grow wafer-scale MoS2 monolayers by MOCVD on sapphire, dry-stamp each 0.7 nm channel plus 3 nm high-k plus 5 nm metal as one 10 nm 'tier sheet', and pattern all tiers with one deep vertical-gate etch (3D NAND style) to get ~1000 lateral 1T1C tiers per 10 um of height.
why: Fact 2 (break-even at 26+ tiers): 1000 tiers at relaxed F~40 nm without EUV gives ~10x bits/cm2 of 2D DRAM; transfer yield per tier is the dominant risk.

title: Magnetosome-chain bond pads self-align dies to 50 nm
idea: Mimic magnetotactic bacteria's magnetite chains: embed CoPt nanomagnet chains under each die's alignment pads and their mirror image on the target wafer, so during die-to-wafer hybrid bonding on a thin water film, magnetic attraction plus capillarity pulls every die into sub-100 nm registration in parallel without a precision bonder.
why: Capital intensity of HBM/3D stacking: parallel self-aligned placement of thousands of dies per minute; bonding capex ~5x lower and finer bond pitch.

title: Iceberg: bitlines built from the wafer backside under 4F2 cells
idea: Most of an iceberg is underwater: build a 4F2 vertical-channel array with capacitors on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to the channel bottoms, and form low-resistance Cu or Ru bitlines on the backside, the way logic now does backside power. No buried bitline has to survive the full front-end thermal budget.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): makes 4F2 practical, a cell 33% smaller than 6F2, without buried-bitline resistance or thermal limits; claim ~30% more bits per wafer at the same F.

title: Sanctioned-fab rule: film-thickness-defined cell replaces litho-defined pitch
idea: Design for a country cut off from EUV, ArF and neon: rotate the cell so every critical dimension is a deposited film thickness (channel length is an epitaxial layer, gate length a wordline film, cell pitch the tier pitch), and the only lithography is a 0.5 um UV-LED step that cuts slits and staircases. The cell is a lateral transistor plus lateral capacitor in each tier, like a rotated 3D NAND page.
why: Removes litho-bound scaling and EUV capital (fact 4): density comes from 64-100 tiers at 0.5 um lithography, roughly halving the 55% depreciation share.

title: Tall silicon pillar as inversion-layer capacitor, no MIM mold
idea: [Box: MOS inversion charge | VCT on the same pillar | charge-share SA | monolithic | single-crystal Si | deep Si pillar etch + ALD high-k/metal plate wrap] Extend each VCT pillar ~1 um downward and wrap the lower section with a high-k/metal plate at fixed bias, so electrons in the sidewall inversion layer form the cell capacitance (~4 fF for a 20 nm pillar at 0.5 nm EOT); single-crystal dark generation (~few e-/s) is negligible against ~25k stored electrons.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): one etched Si feature is both transistor and capacitor, replacing the 70:1 oxide mold + MIM module and cutting masks.

title: Pulsed-laser-crystallized silicon tiers stacked monolithically above periphery
idea: Combine the display industry's laser crystallization with 3D DRAM: deposit amorphous Si for each tier and melt-crystallize only its top ~100 nm with nanosecond pulses from US-made laser sources, keeping lower tiers and CMOS below 400 C and giving near-single-crystal access channels tier by tier.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): monolithic tiers without wafer bonding or Si/SiGe epitaxy (no imported germanium); crystalline mobility for lateral transistors at the cost of one deposition plus laser pass per tier.
